transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

...I guess I'm just here because my family wanted me to come in. It's... mostly just a disagreement we're having. 

Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up. But... I work with data for a living. When I actually compare the timestamps, the missing attachments... and just the way certain community members avoid my questions now... it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. 

But they don't want to hear it, so... they told me to come here.
How long have you felt this way—that people are hiding the truth about your father's death—has it been going on for weeks, or longer?
Longer. It's been... I don't know, about nine months, I guess. Just since the period right after he died, when I had to start sorting through his records and... his messages. That's when I saw it.
Aside from these suspicions, have you ever heard voices or sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice?
No. I don't... hear voices or anything like that. I haven't seen anything that isn't actually there. It's just what's right there in the files.

Before your father passed away, would you say you generally trusted people—friends, coworkers, family—or have you always tended to be wary and suspicious of others' motives, even in unrelated situations?

I... no, I didn't have any issues like that before. I generally trusted people fine. Coworkers, family... it was normal. I didn't go around suspecting everyone of things. It's just... this specific situation. With the files. That's all.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-organized, non-bizarre delusion (belief that family/community members are concealing the truth about his father's death, based on misinterpreted data such as timestamps and missing attachments) persisting for approximately 9 months. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior, no negative symptoms, and no mood episode symptoms reported. Premorbid personality was not paranoid or suspicious, and functioning outside the delusional belief system appears preserved. This pattern is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional psychotic symptoms like hallucinations or disorganization) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no depressive or manic symptoms endorsed).
